table.caption: Verbatim — B.P. Blg. 22, Section 2 (Evidence of knowledge of insufficient funds)
rows: SEC. 2. Evidence of knowledge of insufficient funds.—The making, drawing and issuance of a check payment of which is refused by the drawee because of insufficient funds in or credit with such bank, when presented within ninety (90) days from the date of the check, shall be prima facie evidence of knowledge of such insufficiency of funds or credit unless such maker or drawer pays the holder thereof the amount due thereon, or makes arrangements for payment in full by the drawee of such check within five (5) banking days after receiving notice that such check has not been paid by the drawee.

blocks.markdown: Section 2 creates a **prima facie presumption, not an automatic finding of guilt**. The statutory conditions matter: the check is **presented within 90 days** and dishonored for insufficient funds or credit, and after **notice** that it was not paid, the drawer does not pay or arrange full payment **within five banking days**. The accused may present evidence to **rebut** the presumption.

table.caption: Verbatim — B.P. Blg. 22, Section 4 (Credit construed)
rows: SEC. 4. Credit construed.—The word “credit” as used herein shall be construed to mean an arrangement or understanding with the bank for the payment of such check.

blocks.markdown: **“Credit” does not mean a general promise by another person to pay.** For B.P. Blg. 22, the term refers to an **arrangement or understanding with the drawee bank** for payment of the check.

table.caption: Exam distinction: knowledge
rows: Exam distinction  Do not say that dishonor alone conclusively proves knowledge. Under Lim Lao, the presumption can be rebutted, and actual receipt of notice of dishonor is important to give the drawer the statutory five-banking-day opportunity to pay or arrange payment.
